title: Interested Party vs. Additional Insured: What Your Landlord Actually Needs on Your Renters Insurance
summary: Your lease says to list the landlord on your renters insurance. Here is the difference between an interested party and an additional insured, and which one to pick.
body_markdown:
## **What is an interested party on renters insurance?**


An interested party is a person or company your insurer notifies when your[renters insurance](https://www.safebutler.com/renters-insurance) policy changes, lapses, or is cancelled. That is the whole job. An interested party cannot file a claim on your policy, cannot change your coverage, and receives no payout if something happens to your belongings. For a landlord or property manager, it is simply proof that the insurance they required in the lease is still in force.


Insurers use several names for the same thing. Lemonade calls it an interested party. Liberty Mutual and many agency carriers call it an additional interest. Some leases say "additional interested party." If the person is only supposed to be *told* about your policy, all of these mean the same role.


## **What is an additional insured?**


An additional insured is different. Someone listed as an additional insured is actually covered by your policy, usually for liability only. If a guest is hurt in your apartment and sues both you and the landlord, an additional insured endorsement means your policy can respond on the landlord's behalf as well as yours.


That sounds generous, but it is rarely what either side wants. Your liability limit is shared, so a claim paid for the landlord reduces what is left for you. Most renters carriers will not add a landlord as an additional insured at all, because the landlord already carries their own building and liability policy. If a lease asks for "additional insured" status, it is worth asking the property manager whether they really just need to be notified of cancellation. In our experience that is almost always the answer.


**Interested party vs. additional insured at a glance**


Interested party (additional interest) Additional insured


Gets notified if the policy cancels or lapses Yes Yes


Covered by your liability coverage No Yes


Can file a claim on your policy No Yes, for covered liability


Can change your coverage No No


Shares your coverage limits No Yes


Changes your premium No Sometimes


Commonly accepted by renters insurers Yes Rarely for landlords


What most leases actually need Yes No


## **What landlords actually require**


We maintain lease and insurance details for more than 37,000 apartment communities across the country. Among the 1,008 communities in that dataset whose lease terms require renters insurance, 88 percent ask residents to list the property as an interested party. The rest either leave the wording open or use a phrase like "additional insured" without defining it, which is exactly the confusion this article is about.


The liability requirement is just as consistent. Of the communities that state a minimum, the median is $100,000 of personal liability coverage. Roughly seven in ten specify $100,000 and most of the rest specify $300,000. If your lease is silent on the amount, $100,000 is the figure to assume, and the step up to $300,000 is one of the cheapest upgrades on a renters policy. Our guide to[how much personal property coverage you need](https://www.safebutler.com/blog/how-much-personal-property-coverage-do-you-really-need-in-renters-insurance/) covers the other half of the policy.


Why do landlords care? Two reasons. If a resident causes a fire or a flood that damages the building, the landlord's insurer will look to the resident's liability coverage first. And if a policy quietly lapses, the landlord wants to know before the next incident, not after. The interested party notice solves the second problem without giving the landlord any control over your policy. We wrote about the landlord's side of this in[why landlords should require renters insurance](https://www.safebutler.com/blog/why-landlords-should-require-renters-insurance-understanding-the-key-differences-from-landlord-insurance/) .


## **What information do you need to add an interested party?**


Three things, and your lease or welcome packet usually has all of them:


- The legal name of the owner or management company exactly as the lease wants it listed. This is often not the name on the sign out front.
- A mailing address, which may be a corporate office or a third-party compliance service rather than the leasing office.
- An email address, if the insurer sends electronic notices. Many property managers now use a dedicated insurance compliance inbox.


Check whether the lease names a specific entity such as "XYZ Apartments LLC and its management agent." Entering a nickname or the wrong entity is the most common reason a compliance team rejects an otherwise valid policy.


## **How do you add an interested party?**


If you buy through SafeButler, both of our direct carriers let you enter the landlord's details during checkout. The name and address go straight onto the policy, and the declarations page you receive at purchase already shows them. That is usually what the leasing office wants to see.


If you already have a policy, log in to the insurer's website or app and look for "interested party," "additional interest," or "add landlord" in the policy details. Enter the name and address, save, and download the updated declarations page. Most insurers process the change immediately and send the landlord a confirmation. If you cannot find the option, a quick message to the carrier's support team will do it; this is one of the most routine requests they handle. For a step-by-step look at the process, see[adding your landlord to renters insurance](https://www.safebutler.com/blog/the-benefits-of-adding-your-landlord-to-renters-insurance/) .


Adding an interested party does not change your premium. Our median renters quote across more than 100,000 real quotes in the past year was under $12 a month, and the price is the same with or without a landlord listed.


## **What should you do if the lease says "additional insured"?**


Do not rush to buy an endorsement. Email the property manager and ask one question: "Do you need to be notified if my policy cancels, or do you need liability coverage under my policy?" Nearly every manager will say the first, and listing them as an interested party satisfies it. If they insist on additional insured status, ask your insurer whether it is available. Several carriers simply do not offer it on renters policies, and a lease cannot make an insurer sell a product it does not have. Explaining that to the manager, with the carrier's answer in writing, almost always resolves it.


The one situation where additional insured status genuinely makes sense is a shared house where a roommate or the person on the lease wants coverage under your policy. Even then, a separate policy per renter is usually cleaner. Our list of[common mistakes when buying renters insurance](https://www.safebutler.com/blog/common-mistakes-to-avoid-when-buying-renters-insurance/) goes into this in more detail.


## **Frequently asked questions**


### **Is an interested party the same as additional interest?**


Yes. Interested party, additional interest, and additional interested party are different labels for the same notification-only role. The wording depends on the insurer.


### **Can my landlord see my policy or file a claim if they are an interested party?**


They receive notices about cancellation, non-renewal, and material changes, and they will see the declarations page you give them. They cannot file a claim, collect a payout, or alter your coverage.


### **Does adding my landlord as an interested party cost anything?**


No. It is a free change on every renters policy we are aware of, and it does not affect your premium or deductible. If you are choosing a deductible at the same time, our guide to[picking the right renters insurance deductible](https://www.safebutler.com/blog/how-to-pick-the-right-renters-insurance-deductible-without-regretting-it-later/) can help.


### **What happens if I cancel my policy?**


The insurer notifies the interested party, usually by mail or email, on the cancellation date. Many leases treat a lapse as a lease violation, and some communities enroll you in a more expensive building-provided policy until you show proof of your own. Set the new policy to start before the old one ends.


### **Should the interested party be the owner or the property manager?**


Use whatever the lease specifies. If it does not say, list the entity named as landlord in the lease and ask the leasing office whether the management company should be added too. Many insurers allow more than one interested party.


### **My landlord asked for a certificate of insurance. Is that different?**


Usually not for renters. The declarations page that shows your name, the address, your coverage limits, and the interested party is what most apartment communities mean by "certificate" or "proof of insurance." If they require a formal certificate, your insurer can issue one on request.
